newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EU chief negotiator says telecoms deal on track.
newsitem.headline: EU chief negotiator says telecoms deal on track.

text.p: The European Union's chief negotiator to global telecoms talks said he saw no major obstacles left to clinching a pact to liberalise the $600 billion telecommunications market by a Saturday deadline.
"We think we can relatively confidently say that we look forward to a successful conclusion to the talks by the end of this week," Karl Falkenberg told reporters in Geneva on Wednesday.
Falkenberg said major trading partners were still looking for some improvements in proposals from the developing world but that the main problems appeared to have been solved.
"I don't expect any difficulties as long as everything that is on the table today is on the table on Saturday," he said.
The EU official also said he thought Washington would not block the deal out of discontent with Canada's decision to prevent majority foreign ownership of its domestic telecoms firms.

"I think the United States is coming round to a more rational approach. Canada is opening access to its markets in a different number of ways. I have the impression we are not going to see this issue become a deal-breaker," he said.

U.S. Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang told reporters on Monday that Washington was unhappy that Canada only allowed foreignors to hold a maximum 46.7 percent of equity capital in domestic telecom firms.

Senior Canadian officials said on Wednesday that Canada was unlikely to backpedal from its position on foreign ownership but added they would instead offer to relax rules on domestic satellite communications.

Some 59 governments representing more than 90 per cent of the global market have submitted offers to open their domestic telecom markets to foreign operators. Sri Lanka and Tanzania were expected to present offers by the end of the week.

U.S. negotiators are now assessing whether they have the "critical mass" of quality offers Washington says it needs before it will guarantee unfettered foreign access to is own telecoms market, the world's biggest.
The United States derailed an effort last April to reach a global pact, saying offers from emerging economies were insufficient.
